newsitem.title: USA: U.S. broadens its probe of looted Nazi gold.
newsitem.headline: U.S. broadens its probe of looted Nazi gold.

text.p: President Bill Clinton has ordered a broad inter-agency investigation of the U.S. role in the seizure and disposition of Nazi and other assets after the second World War, including how neutral Switzerland handled the issue, a Jewish group said on Monday.

In a letter to the World Jewish Congress made public by the group, Clinton said an interim report will be completed in the next few months and that he will "make it a priority to declassify and make available to the public the relevant documentary materials."

The president named Ambassador Stuart Eizenstat, the special envoy for property restitution in Central and Eastern Europe, to oversee the inter-agency investigation which is an extension of one already undertaken by the U.S. State Department and the Holocaust Museum.

In a letter to WJC President Edgar Bronfman, released by the group, Clinton said, "I share your view of the importance of an expeditious and thorough review of dormant accounts and other Nazi assets in Switzerland and I am pleased that the Swiss government has begun this process."

He added, "As you know, the subject of allied and neutral nation actions during and after the war to handle Nazi assets and dormant accounts is both important and complex. I have asked Ambassador Eizenstat to look into the matter thoroughly."

The World Jewish Congress and the U.S. Senate Banking Committee have been combing the U.S. National Archives for documents relating to assets looted by the Nazis, uncovering warnings from U.S. government officials that the Swiss had received more looted Nazi gold than they admitted in post-war negotiations.
Banking Committee Chairman Alfonse D'Amato, a New York Republican, asked that the State Department review U.S. treaties with Switzerland on the issue.
